questions.question: What kind of function is a norm on a vector space $\boldsymbol{V}$?
options: A function $\|\cdot\|\colon \boldsymbol{V}\to[0,+\infty)$ satisfying the norm axioms.
A scalar product that must be linear in both arguments.
A metric that is defined on arbitrary pairs without reference to vectors.
questions.explanation: A norm assigns each vector a nonnegative length obeying definiteness, homogeneity $\|cv\|=|c|\|v\|$, and the triangle inequality; these axioms make it a function $\|\cdot\|:V\to[0,\infty)$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: A function $\boldsymbol{V}\to\boldsymbol{V}$ has the wrong codomain; norms return nonnegative scalars.
A scalar product linear in both arguments is an inner product, not a norm.
A norm is defined using the vector-space structure, not arbitrary pairs.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which statement is the best interpretation of a normed vector space?
options: It is a vector space equipped with a rule assigning consistent lengths to vectors.
It is any metric space, even without vector addition or scalar multiplication.
It is a vector space in which all vectors have norm $1$.
It is a vector space where the triangle inequality is replaced by equality.
